claims.text: Introducing cation vacancies or dopants into transition-metal oxide electrocatalysts alters their electronic structure.
Cation vacancies or dopants redistribute charge locally within the catalyst lattice.
The resulting electronic and charge redistribution optimizes the adsorption energy of oxygen intermediates.
Cation tuning enhances catalytic activity for oxygen reactions.
The baseline is a pristine transition-metal oxide catalyst without engineered cation vacancies or dopants.
Cation-tuning engineering can be implemented through cation vacancies or cation doping.
ORR and OER, including applications in Zn-air batteries, are relevant testing contexts for cation-tuned transition-metal catalysts.
Fuel-cell environments and unspecified standard pH and temperature ranges are appropriate conditions for the proposed comparison.
The engineered vacancies or dopants are the structural mediator responsible for modifying electronic structure and local charge distribution.
Optimized binding energies of oxygen intermediates facilitate multistep electron-transfer reactions.
Facilitating multistep electron transfer through altered intermediate binding enhances reaction kinetics.
Relative to a pristine catalyst, a cation-tuned catalyst will have lower overpotential.
Relative to a pristine catalyst, a cation-tuned catalyst will have higher current density.
Lower overpotential or higher current density would indicate more efficient oxygen adsorption and reaction kinetics.
The proposed relationship is expected to apply to transition-metal oxides during ORR and OER.
The effect may be negligible in other catalytic systems or reaction environments.
The magnitude of improvement and optimal vacancy or dopant level depend on the particular oxide and reaction conditions.
